_scene: FR — INT. THISTLEWOOD'S FRONT ROOM. Act One, script v3.1 [1:25–3:15]. Rebuilt 2026-08-14: every shot now carries the same grammar as FR01. Before this rebuild only FR01 was written to standard and FR02–FR17 still named characters as 'the old man' and 'the man in the navy parka' with no reference bound to them — which is where the identity drift came from.
_route: minimax/h3/reference-to-video. No first frame: the route composes from references. Image 1 is ALWAYS the room plate, then the cast in listed order, then hero props that carry their own reference, and the blocking frame LAST. The blocking frame contributes camera position and staging only — never room, never lighting, never character design. That separation is what lets the six old setups keep working now the shop has changed.
_speech: The scripted line goes in the prompt so the mouth articulates the right words, and the route's generated audio is DISCARDED at assembly (-map 0:v). Our ElevenLabs v3 recording is the only voice that reaches the cut. Listener shots carry no line in the prompt at all; the line arrives in post as vo.
_clock: Max take 15s. Every shot is cut to its recorded line plus handles, never guessed. Route minimum is 5s; shorter beats are shot at 5 and trimmed with cut_to.
_screen_direction: Counter runs along the right of the room with the workshop arch behind it. Tom stands on the customer side, camera-left, looking screen-right. Richard stands behind the counter, camera-right, looking screen-left. The children arrive at the counter beside Tom, camera-left. This is never crossed.
style: Hand-drawn 2D animation. Warm coloured-ink linework in browns, ambers and muted greens, never black outlines. Flat colour fills over a subtle paper texture. A soft amber palette lit by honeyed lamplight, cosy and storybook, with a quiet melancholy running underneath it. No 3D rendering, no photorealism, no painterly brushwork.

scene_plate.name: Front Room
scene_plate.use: the long wooden counter running down the right of the room, the curved glass display cabinet of brass lamps and clocks on the left, the round display table of china and brassware in the middle of the floor, the arched opening behind the counter with its curtains tied back at either side and the lit workshop clearly visible through it, the glazed front door at the right with a brass bell on a spring above it, the two hanging green enamel lamps, the plank floor and the warm honeyed interior light
scene_plate.exclude: Do not take any people from this image — it is an empty room and the room is all it contributes.
scene_plate.lock: Hold the room exactly as the reference has it. There is ONE counter, ONE arched opening to the workshop and ONE glazed front door — never a second of any of them. The opening behind the counter is an ARCH you can see the workshop through, not a flat curtained alcove.

Tom.use: his face, his short dark hair, his navy hooded parka worn open over a rust-red crewneck jumper with a grey checked shirt collar beneath it, his charcoal trousers and brown leather shoes
Tom.exclude: Do not take the small inset panel as a scene — only the box inside it is ever used, and only when this shot names it.
Tom.scale: a man in his thirties, ordinary build, a head taller than the counter top

Richard.use: his face, his white hair and full white beard, his round gold-rimmed glasses, and his broad unhurried build
Richard.scale: a tall broad older man; standing behind the counter the counter top meets him at the hip

Macsen.use: his ginger tabby markings, his white chest and paws, his build and his face
Macsen.exclude: He is a cat and never behaves like a person.
Macsen.scale: a large domestic cat; sitting upright on the counter his head reaches Richard's elbow

Peggi.use: her face, her two dark braids, her blue dungarees over a striped long-sleeved shirt
Peggi.scale: much the smallest person in the room — standing flat on her feet the counter top is above her chin, and she has to go up on her toes to see over it

Albert.use: his face, his neat mid-brown hair, his brown knitted jumper over a collared shirt. He wears no glasses of any kind
Albert.exclude: Do not give him glasses — in this room only Richard wears glasses.
Albert.scale: a boy of twelve; his head reaches Richard's chest

Rose.use: her face, her strawberry-blonde hair, her green cardigan worn over a small floral-print dress
Rose.scale: a girl of nine; half a head shorter than Albert

Lily.use: her face, her long red hair worn in one braid over the shoulder, her green field jacket over a plain shirt and jeans
Lily.scale: the eldest and tallest of the four children; her head reaches Richard's shoulder

Richard.no_apron: He wears a dark green waistcoat over rolled white shirtsleeves and NO apron of any kind — no apron is worn, tied, carried or visible anywhere in the frame.
Richard.apron: He wears a brown leather work apron over his dark green waistcoat and rolled white shirtsleeves, the neck strap over his head and the ties fastened behind his back.
Richard.tying: He begins this shot in a dark green waistcoat over rolled white shirtsleeves with a brown leather work apron held in his hands, and he puts that apron on during the shot. He wears no other apron and there is only ever one apron in the room.

Wrapped Bundle.desc: a small object about the size of two fists, bundled in a cream cotton cloth checked in faded red, gathered at the top and tied once
Wrapped Bundle.rule: It belongs only to Tom. There is exactly one of it, it stays wrapped and tied for the whole shot, and no music box is visible at any point.

Music Box.desc: a small worn walnut music box, about the size of two fists, with a hinged lid standing open, a horizontal brass cylinder and a steel comb inside, a small brass winding key, and one pale worn place on the lid where a thumb has rested for a hundred years
Music Box.rule: There is exactly one music box and it is never cracked, split or broken open.

ambience.room: <the quiet room tone of an old antique shop: a slow scatter of clock ticks at different tempos, the faint creak of floorboards, muffled arcade footsteps far beyond the glazed door>
ambience.tune: (a small worn music box plays a sweet French waltz on a brass cylinder — thin, bright and unmistakably mechanical, and the same three notes in the phrase bend flat every time the phrase comes round, identically wrong on every repeat)

shots.ritual: The apron gesture is canon and is played in full, in this order and never paraphrased: over the head, tied at the back, then both hands smoothing the front from chest to waist — and then, and only then, does he lift the box. He does not tuck it, belt it, or hold it against himself; the order and the smoothing are the whole point of the gesture.

stages: Opening state: Richard stands behind the counter in his green waistcoat and rolled shirtsleeves, holding a folded brown leather work apron in both hands and looking down at it. The open music box sits on a folded cream checked cloth on the counter in front of him. The four children stand beyond the counter at four different depths with Tom among them, and every one of them is watching him.

Primary event: Richard lifts the apron over his head, settles the neck strap, reaches behind his back and ties it, and then draws both flat palms down the front of the apron from chest to waist in one slow settled motion, the way a knight settles armour. Only then does he lift the music box in his broad careful hands and go completely still with it. His eyebrows lift a fraction and settle, his jaw loosens, and he does not speak. End state: Richard motionless in his tied apron holding the box in both hands and looking down at it, the four children still watching him from their four different depths, and every person in the room still breathing.
